name: Israel
traditionNote: A mixed system with a common-law spine: statutes are the starting point, but a rule laid down by the Supreme Court binds every lower court, so the case law matters as much as the text. Layered on top of Ottoman and British Mandate remnants, and alongside it the rabbinical, sharia, Druze and recognised Christian courts apply religious law in matters of personal status.
summary: The Knesset, a single chamber of 120 members, is the only body that makes primary legislation, and it also acts as the constituent authority that enacts Basic Laws. A bill passes three readings, is signed by the President of the State, the Prime Minister, the Speaker and the minister charged with its implementation, and becomes law when it is published in Reshumot, the official gazette, in the series Sefer HaChukkim. Unless the statute provides otherwise it comes into force on the day of that publication. Secondary legislation - regulations, orders and rules made by ministers under an enabling statute - is published in the same gazette in Kovetz HaTakanot, municipal by-laws in the local-government edition of it, and appointments, tenders and statutory notices in Yalkut HaPirsumim. The authentic text is the Hebrew text as it appears in Reshumot: the consolidated version of a statute in the Knesset's national legislation database is an editorial convenience, and so is every commercial one. There is no single constitutional document. Thirteen Basic Laws stand in place of one, some with entrenched clauses requiring a special majority and some with limitation clauses against which ordinary statutes can be measured, and in January 2024 the Supreme Court held that it may itself review a Basic Law in extreme cases.
hierarchy: Basic Laws, enacted by the Knesset acting as constituent authority; only some are entrenched, and the Supreme Court claims a power to review them in exceptional cases
Statutes of the Knesset (חוקים), including Mandatory ordinances still in force and their consolidated Nusach Chadash versions
Emergency regulations made by the Government, which can suspend or vary a statute for a limited period while the declared state of emergency lasts
Regulations, orders and rules made by ministers under an enabling statute (חקיקת משנה), published in Kovetz HaTakanot
By-laws of municipalities, local councils and regional councils (חוקי עזר), approved by the Interior Ministry and published in the local-government edition of Kovetz HaTakanot
Binding precedent: a rule laid down by the Supreme Court binds every other court but not the Supreme Court itself (Basic Law: The Judiciary, section 20)
Religious law, applied by the rabbinical, sharia, Druze and recognised Christian courts within their personal-status jurisdiction
Where a question has no answer in any of these: analogy, and failing that the principles of freedom, justice, equity and peace of Israel's heritage (Foundations of Law Act, 1980)

gazette.name: Reshumot
gazette.en: Records - the Official Gazette of the State of Israel
gazette.authority: Reshumot Department, Ministry of Justice (מחלקת רשומות, משרד המשפטים)
gazette.coverage: התש״ח (1948) to the present; the archive is browsable by Hebrew year from the state's founding year onwards, for every series the department edits
gazette.desc: The single channel through which an instrument becomes binding, published in named series: ספר החוקים (Sefer HaChukkim, statutes of the Knesset), קובץ התקנות (Kovetz HaTakanot, regulations and orders) with its separate editions for local-government enactments and for customs, purchase tax and compulsory-payment rates, הצעות חוק הממשלה (government bills), and ילקוט הפרסומים (Yalkut HaPirsumim, appointments, statutory notices, company and partnership notices). The department also publishes the דיני מדינת ישראל: נוסח חדש consolidations of Mandatory-era ordinances, the historical English translations of Israeli law, and the מפתח תחיקה index to all primary legislation from 1948 to 1997, which reaches back over Mandatory ordinances, Orders in Council, the Defence Regulations and Ottoman legislation.
gazette.howto: The landing page lists every series with a one-line description, and each name opens the same archive filtered to that series. To find a particular issue go to פרסומי רשומות and search by סוג חוברת (series), מספר חוברת (issue number), תוכן עניינים (contents), שנה עברית (Hebrew year), חיפוש בחוברת (text within the issue) or a publication-date range; you must set at least one field before it returns anything. Bear in mind that a citation to an Israeli statute gives the series, issue number and page, and that the year in the statute's own name is the Hebrew year, so the Hebrew-year filter is usually the fastest way in.
gazette.note: Free to read and download, no account. Only the Hebrew text published here is authentic; an Arabic or English version of the same instrument, wherever it appears, is a translation.

constitution.name: Basic Laws of the State of Israel
constitution.coverage: Thirteen Basic Laws, from Basic Law: The Knesset (1958) to Basic Law: Israel - the Nation State of the Jewish People (2018), each with its English text
constitution.desc: Israel has no codified constitution, and this is the official account of what stands in its place. When the Constituent Assembly could not agree on one in 1950, the Harari resolution settled on legislating the constitution chapter by chapter instead; the chapters are the Basic Laws, and they were never gathered into a single document. The Knesset's page introduces each one, says when and by which Knesset it was passed, notes whether it contains an entrenched clause, and links the English text. The Declaration of Independence, on the same site, is not a Basic Law and is not enforceable as one, but the courts read it as a statement of the state's founding principles.
constitution.howto: Read the introduction first: it sets out the unresolved argument about whether Basic Laws outrank ordinary statutes at all, then lists the Basic Laws in order of enactment with a PDF of each in English. For the authoritative Hebrew text of any of them, including amendments made since, look the Basic Law up in the Knesset's national legislation database or in the Sefer HaChukkim issue that published it.
constitution.note: The English texts here are the Knesset's own translations and are for information; the Hebrew text published in Reshumot governs. Two Basic Laws, Human Dignity and Liberty and Freedom of Occupation, carry limitation clauses, and it is against those two that the courts have struck down ordinary statutes since 1995.

sources.name: Pirsumei Reshumot
sources.coverage: Every series edited by the department, by Hebrew year, from התש״ח (1948) onwards
sources.desc: The searchable face of the gazette: the scanned issues themselves, as PDFs, which is where you confirm that a statute or regulation says what a database claims it says, and on what date it was promulgated.
sources.howto: Choose the series in סוג חוברת, then narrow by issue number, Hebrew year or publication-date range; חיפוש בחוברת searches text inside the issues and תוכן עניינים searches the tables of contents. Nothing is returned until at least one field is set. Results are individual issues, so you may open a booklet and still have to find the instrument on the page cited.
sources.note: Older issues are scans rather than born-digital text, so text search over them is only as good as the scanning; when in doubt, browse by year and issue number instead of searching.

sources.name: Hukei Medinat Yisrael
sources.en: Laws of the State of Israel, in the National Legislation Database
sources.coverage: Primary legislation in force and repealed, with the legislative history of each statute from the original enactment through every amendment
sources.desc: The official consolidated text of Israeli statutes, and the first place to read a law rather than the issue of the gazette that made it. Each statute carries its subject classification, the committee that handled it, the minister responsible for implementation, its Reshumot publication reference and the chain of amending laws behind the current wording.
sources.howto: Search מילה מתוך השם for a word in the title, or filter by מספר כנסת (which Knesset passed it), תוקף (in force or not), נושא (subject), ועדה מטפלת (handling committee), שר או שרה ממונים (responsible minister) and a Reshumot publication-date range. The result list exports to Excel with ייצוא לקובץ Excel, which is the nearest thing to bulk access. חיפוש מתקדם adds full-text search across the databases.
sources.note: The third database in the same system, חקיקת משנה (secondary legislation), is still marked המאגר בהקמה - under construction - so regulations and orders are not reliably here; for those, go to Kovetz HaTakanot in the gazette or to a commercial database.

sources.name: Hatza'ot Hok
sources.coverage: Bills of the current and previous Knessets, including bills that were stopped, frozen or dropped when a Knesset dissolved
sources.desc: Where a law lives before it is a law. Every private member's, committee and government bill with its type, its handling committee and its position in the process - tabled, preliminary reading, first reading, committee, second and third readings, passed - and the text at each stage. The database home also carries a live count of the current Knesset's pipeline, from bills tabled to laws passed.
sources.howto: The view opens on the current Knesset; change מספר כנסת to look at an earlier one, or filter by סוג הצעת חוק (government, private member's, committee), ועדה מטפלת and מצב הצעת חוק (status). A bill that passed links through to its published text; a bill that did not simply stops where it stopped.
sources.note: A government bill is also published in the gazette, in the הצעות חוק הממשלה series, and that published version is the citable one. Bill text is superseded the moment the committee amends it.

sources.name: Knesset plenum sessions
sources.coverage: Plenum sittings by year and month, several thousand per Knesset term; committee protocols are published in a parallel section of the same site
sources.desc: The verbatim record of the plenum, and the standard source for what a minister said a clause was for. Sittings are listed by date with their agenda items, so a reading of a particular bill can be found by the sitting that held it.
sources.howto: Pick the year and month from the timeline, then narrow with מילה בכותרת הנושא (word in the item title) or מילות מפתח (keywords). Each sitting opens to its items and the protocol text; the parallel committee-protocol search covers the committee stage, which is usually where a bill actually changed.
sources.note: Hebrew only, and the protocol is a record of debate, not of law: nothing said in it changes the text that was eventually published.

sources.name: Atar HaHakika HaMemshalti
sources.desc: The pre-legislative stage, published for public comment: תזכירי חוק (draft bills circulated by a ministry before they reach the Government), draft secondary legislation, draft support criteria and draft administrative procedures. It is the only public window on a measure between the moment a ministry drafts it and the moment it is tabled.
sources.coverage: Draft memoranda and draft subordinate instruments currently open for comment, plus the archive of closed consultations
sources.howto: Search free text, or filter to תזכירי חוק, טיוטות חקיקת משנה, טיוטות מבחני תמיכה or טיוטות נהלים. Each item shows the publishing ministry, the comment deadline and the draft document; registration adds email alerts on new drafts.
sources.note: Everything here is a draft with no legal force, and a draft may be published, amended out of recognition and never enacted. Comment periods are short, often three weeks. The root address redirects to a locale-specific entry point (/s/?language=iw), which is why a link checker reports it as a redirect; the root is the address to keep.

sources.name: Supreme Court judgments and decisions
sources.native: החלטות ופסקי דין של בית המשפט העליון
sources.en: Search of Supreme Court judgments and decisions
sources.coverage: Judgments and decisions given from 1997 onwards, and judgments published in the official Piskei Din reports from volume 61 (2006) onwards
sources.desc: The official free archive of the court that matters most in Israeli law, sitting both as the highest court of appeal and as the High Court of Justice. Its rulings bind every other court, so this is where a proposition of Israeli law is confirmed or lost.
sources.howto: Search free text, or by case number - the toggle חדש/ישן switches between the current numbering and the pre-2011 form, and you enter the case number, month and year separately. Narrow by document date, by document type, by judge, party or advocate, or tick פסיקה נבחרת to see only the selected reported decisions. Case numbers carry their court prefix: בג״ץ for the High Court of Justice, ע״א for a civil appeal, ע״פ for a criminal one.
sources.note: Decisions before 1997 are not here; for those you need the printed Piskei Din reports or a commercial database. The site does not carry lower-court judgments at all.

sources.name: Supreme Court of Israel - judgments in English
sources.en: Judgments of the Supreme Court of Israel, translated
sources.coverage: Selected judgments and decisions translated into English, with selected summaries, from Piskei Din volume 50 onwards
sources.desc: The court's own English window, and the only official English source for Israeli case law. It is explicitly a selection: the court translates judgments it considers of wider interest, so absence from this database says nothing about the importance of a case in Israeli law.
sources.howto: Search by term or case number, with a separate filter for the date the translation was published as against the date of judgment, and by document type and length. If the case you want is not here, try Versa, which translates a different selection, and otherwise read the Hebrew original in the main database.
sources.note: Translations are provided for convenience and the Hebrew judgment governs. The English site is a small fraction of the Hebrew database.

sources.name: Judgments distributed by the courts spokesperson
sources.native: פסקי דין והחלטות שהופצו על ידי מערך הדוברות
sources.en: Judgments and decisions of public interest
sources.coverage: Over 11,000 judgments and decisions of public interest across all instances, released as they are given
sources.desc: The nearest thing to a free official source for judgments below the Supreme Court. District, magistrates', family, labour, traffic, juvenile, small-claims and local-affairs courts all appear here - but only the decisions the spokesperson's office chose to release, usually with a summary attached.
sources.howto: Filter by סוג ההליך (civil, criminal, family, administrative, labour, traffic, juvenile, parole boards, or בג״ץ), by court and by district. Each entry gives the case number, the bench, the date and PDFs of the judgment and its summary. The case number is the key to finding the full decision elsewhere.
sources.note: A selection, not a database: the page itself says the complete body of judgments and decisions is in Net HaMishpat, which needs an Israeli digital identity to enter.

sources.name: Net HaMishpat
sources.coverage: All case files of the general courts and the labour courts, including publishable copies of decisions from closed proceedings such as family and juvenile cases
sources.desc: The system through which Israeli litigation actually runs: filing, service, reading the file and reading every decision in it. It is also, on the judiciary's own account, where the complete body of judgments and decisions can be found - which makes it the official answer to a question the free databases only partly answer.
sources.howto: Entry is through the national digital identity service (מערכת ההזדהות הלאומית) or a smart card, with separate paths for unrepresented parties, lawyers and their clients, corporations, and witnesses or experts who are not parties. This guide is the official walkthrough of registration and of filing, receiving and reading documents.
sources.note: In practice closed to anyone without an Israeli identity number, which is why researchers outside Israel fall back on the spokesperson's collection or a commercial database.

sources.name: The Judicial Authority
sources.coverage: The whole court system: Supreme Court, district courts, magistrates' courts, family, labour, juvenile, traffic, local-affairs, small-claims and community courts
sources.desc: The judiciary's home page, which is where the structure of the system is set out: three general instances - magistrates', district, Supreme - with specialised courts alongside them, and the labour courts as a separate two-instance track. It also carries court fees, filing services, the parole boards and the links into the two judgment databases.
sources.howto: Use קישורים חשובים at the top for the two decision databases and for Net HaMishpat; נושאים lists each type of court, with its jurisdiction and its locations. For an English overview, the Supreme Court's own English site is more complete than the English side of this page.
sources.note: The judiciary's old domain, www.court.gov.il, currently serves only an out-of-service notice pointing here, so older links and citations to it are broken. supreme.court.gov.il and supremedecisions.court.gov.il still work.

sources.name: Rabbinical courts judgments
sources.coverage: Around 3,400 published judgments of the twelve regional rabbinical courts and the Great Rabbinical Court
sources.desc: Marriage and divorce between Jews in Israel are matters for the rabbinical courts, not the civil ones, and this is their published case law: agunot and permission to remarry, the ketubah and divorce compensation, maintenance, custody, property division, conversion and personal status. It is where Jewish law is applied as state law.
sources.howto: Filter by בית דין (the regional court, or הגדול for the appellate Great Rabbinical Court), by נושא (subject) and by תת נושא. Each entry gives the case number, the dayanim who sat, the date, the advocates and, for many, a summary of the ruling.
sources.note: A published selection rather than the complete output of the courts, and Hebrew only. Jurisdiction over some of these matters is shared with the family courts, so the same dispute may generate parallel civil and rabbinical proceedings.

sources.name: Sharia courts judgments
sources.authority: The Sharia Courts, Ministry of Justice
sources.coverage: Over 5,000 decisions of the regional sharia courts - Jerusalem, Jaffa, Haifa, Acre, Nazareth, Taibe, Baqa al-Gharbiyye, Sakhnin, Beer Sheva - and the Sharia Court of Appeals
sources.desc: The state's sharia courts, inherited from the Ottoman and Mandate systems and recognised by the Law and Administration Ordinance, decide personal status for Muslim citizens: marriage, divorce, khul', maintenance, custody, guardianship, wills and inheritance, and waqf. Their published decisions are here.
sources.howto: Filter by נושא (subject) and by בית הדין, including השרעי לערעורים for the appeal court. Entries carry the case number, subject, court and date of decision, with the decision document attached.
sources.note: Parallel systems exist for the Druze courts and for the recognised Christian communities, whose decisions are not collected in a comparable public database.

sources.name: Ma'agar Kitvei Amana
sources.authority: International Law Department, Ministry of Justice
sources.coverage: Around 1,300 scanned treaty instruments signed or ratified by Israel from 1948 onwards; the scanning is an ongoing project and the database is not yet complete
sources.desc: The official collection of Israel's Kitvei Amana - the treaty series - being digitised instrument by instrument. It runs from the 1949 armistice agreements and the early multilateral conventions through bilateral tax, trade and cooperation agreements.
sources.howto: Search by the treaty's full name, by its treaty number, or by a word from the Hebrew title. The date shown beside a file is the date it was uploaded, not the date of signature, ratification or entry into force - read the instrument itself for those.
sources.note: The database itself says questions about the legal status and validity of a published treaty go to the Treaties Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Israel is dualist: a treaty binds the state internationally but does not become domestic law until the Knesset legislates it, though customary international law is absorbed directly.

sources.name: Meida Mishpati
sources.authority: Government of Israel (all ministries and authorities)
sources.coverage: Over 18,000 items from every ministry, regulator and statutory authority
sources.desc: Where the executive branch's own legal output collects: administrative guidelines and draft guidelines, exemptions and decisions under regulatory statutes, registrars' decisions, disciplinary tribunal judgments, case-law digests and copies of the regulations a given authority administers. Much of the operative detail of Israeli regulation is here rather than in any statute.
sources.howto: Filter by משרד (ministry or authority), סוג מידע משפטי (type - guidelines, regulations, registrar decisions, judgments, digests), ערכאה, subject, audience or date range. It is a cross-government feed, so narrowing by the responsible authority first is usually faster than searching text.
sources.note: Guidance published here is administrative, not legislative: it binds the authority that issued it and can be challenged, but it is not the law itself. Only what appears in Kovetz HaTakanot is secondary legislation.

sources.name: Nevo
sources.authority: Nevo Publishing Ltd (הוצאה לאור נבו), a private publisher
sources.coverage: Over 14 million judgments and decisions, plus legislation from the Mandate onwards, treaties, legal literature and pleadings
sources.desc: Not an official publisher, but the database Israeli practitioners actually open. It carries the full run of court and tribunal decisions the free official sites do not, the consolidated legislation with its amendment history, and since 1997 it has been the publisher of the official Piskei Din reports of the Supreme Court. It is listed here because a search for Israeli case law that avoids it is not a serious search.
sources.howto: The top navigation splits into פסיקה (case law), חקיקה (legislation), ספרות (literature) and specialist collections. Subscription is by module and priced per user; university and bar-association members often reach it through an institutional login rather than a personal one.
sources.note: Private and paywalled, and its consolidated texts are an editorial product like any other. Its case coverage is the reason to use it, not any official status.

sources.name: Versa - Cardozo Israeli Supreme Court Project
sources.authority: Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law, Yeshiva University
sources.coverage: Several hundred translated opinions, weighted to constitutional and administrative law, with topic collections including Jewish law and family law
sources.desc: An academic English archive of landmark Israeli Supreme Court opinions, translated and annotated, with editorial commentary on major decisions. For the constitutional cases - judicial review of Basic Laws, the reasonableness amendment, security and rights - it is fuller and better organised than the court's own English selection.
sources.howto: Browse by topic or search the translated opinions; each case page gives the case number, the date, the bench and the translated text, often with a summary and links to commentary.
sources.note: Unofficial translations by a foreign law school, however careful. Cite the Hebrew judgment.

sources.name: WIPO Lex - Israel
sources.coverage: Israeli intellectual-property statutes and regulations, with related constitutional and enforcement texts, in Hebrew and in English translation
sources.desc: A practical way around the absence of systematic official translation, for one subject area. WIPO Lex holds the Israeli IP legislation in English translation alongside the Hebrew, with the treaty memberships that sit behind it.
sources.howto: Open the Israel member profile and browse the legislation list; each entry links the text in the available languages and notes the instrument it amends or implements.
sources.note: Translations are supplied for information by an international organisation, not by Israel, and can lag amendments by years.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of a statute
findLaw.steps: Search a word from the title in חוקי מדינת ישראל, the laws database inside the Knesset's national legislation database, and open the statute. The page gives the consolidated text with the chain of amendments behind it and the Reshumot reference for each. Where the wording matters, follow that reference into the gazette issue and read the published text.
findLaw.source: Hukei Medinat Yisrael (חוקי מדינת ישראל), the Knesset

findLaw.task: Confirm what was actually published, and when it took effect
findLaw.steps: Go to פרסומי רשומות, set סוג חוברת to the series - ספר החוקים for a statute, קובץ התקנות for a regulation - and narrow by Hebrew year or issue number from the citation. Open the PDF and read the instrument's own commencement provision; absent one, it came into force on the day of publication.

findLaw.task: Find a regulation, order or rule
findLaw.steps: Look in Kovetz HaTakanot in the gazette archive, by year and issue number, since the Knesset's secondary-legislation database is still under construction. If the instrument is recent and you only know the ministry, check מידע משפטי filtered to that authority, and for a draft not yet made, the government legislation site.

findLaw.task: Look up a Supreme Court judgment
findLaw.steps: Search the case number in the Supreme Court's judgment database, switching the חדש/ישן toggle to match the numbering format, or search party names and terms. Tick פסיקה נבחרת to restrict the results to the reported decisions. Coverage starts in 1997; anything earlier needs the printed Piskei Din or a commercial database.
findLaw.source: Supreme Court judgments and decisions, The Judicial Authority

findLaw.task: Find a judgment of a lower court
findLaw.steps: Start with the spokesperson's collection and filter by court, district and type of proceeding - it is a selection of decisions of public interest, but it is free and it covers every instance. If the case is not there, the full record is in Net HaMishpat, which requires an Israeli digital identity, or in Nevo, which is paid.
findLaw.source: Judgments distributed by the courts spokesperson, The Judicial Authority

findLaw.task: Track a bill through the Knesset
findLaw.steps: Open the bills database, set מספר כנסת to the Knesset in question and filter by status or by handling committee. The entry shows the bill type, where it stopped or how far it got, and the text at each stage; the debate itself is in the plenum and committee protocols on the same site.

findLaw.task: Find a treaty Israel is party to
findLaw.steps: Search the treaty database by name, treaty number or a Hebrew keyword and open the scanned instrument. Treat the date on the listing as the upload date only, and take questions of entry into force or current validity to the Treaties Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Remember that a treaty does not apply as domestic law until the Knesset legislates it.
findLaw.source: Ma'agar Kitvei Amana (מאגר כתבי אמנה), Ministry of Justice

findLaw.steps: There is no current official English text of Israeli legislation. Start with the Knesset's English Basic Laws for constitutional material, the Supreme Court's English judgment database and Versa for case law, and WIPO Lex for intellectual property. The Ministry of Justice's own English translation series in the gazette stops in 1981, and the English Sefer HaChukkim in 1990; anything more recent is unofficial and needs checking against the Hebrew.
findLaw.source: Basic Laws in English, the Knesset

subnational: Israel is a unitary state with no federal tier: there are no state or provincial legislatures, and all primary legislation is the Knesset's. Below it, municipalities, local councils and regional councils make by-laws (חוקי עזר) under the Municipalities Ordinance and the Local Councils Ordinance; these require the Interior Ministry's approval and are published in the local-government edition of Kovetz HaTakanot, which is the publication that gives them effect. The Interior Ministry maintains a consolidated by-laws database, but it is not the authoritative text and it refuses connections from outside Israel, so in practice you either read the gazette or the copy the authority itself publishes on its own site. Separately, and outside this structure entirely, military legislation issued by the IDF area commander applies in the West Bank and is published not in Reshumot but in the Kovetz Manasharim, Tzavim u-Minuyim (קובץ מנשרים, צווים ומינויים), which has no comprehensive free online edition; the Military Advocate General's site publishes individual security orders. Israeli law was extended by statute to East Jerusalem and, by the Golan Heights Law of 1981, to the Golan; the UN Security Council has declared those measures without international legal effect, and this record takes no position beyond noting where each body of law is published.
caveats: The authentic text of any Israeli instrument is the Hebrew text in the Reshumot issue that published it. The Knesset's consolidated statute text is an official convenience but still an editorial product, its secondary-legislation database is openly marked as under construction, and every commercial consolidation is a private one. Free official case law is thin below the Supreme Court: the Supreme Court's own database starts in 1997, the spokesperson's collection is an explicit selection of decisions of public interest, and the complete record sits in Net HaMishpat behind an Israeli digital identity - which is why Nevo and Takdin, both private and paywalled, are what practitioners use, and Takdin refuses connections from outside Israel altogether. English is a real gap: the official translation series ended in 1981 and 1990, the Knesset's Basic Law translations and the Supreme Court's translated judgments are selections offered for information, and Versa, WIPO Lex and Constitute are unofficial. The treaty database is an unfinished scanning project whose displayed dates are upload dates, and treaty status questions belong to the Foreign Ministry, not to it. Guidance and administrative directives published on gov.il bind the authority that issued them but are not legislation. Two structural points are easy to miss: a state of emergency has been declared continuously since 1948, which keeps the power to make emergency regulations that vary a statute permanently available, and there is no codified constitution, so the constitutional question in any given case is which Basic Law applies, whether it is entrenched, and whether the Supreme Court - which held in January 2024 that it may review Basic Laws in extreme cases - would treat it as reviewable at all. Finally, the judiciary's old domain www.court.gov.il now serves only an out-of-service notice, so older citations to it are dead.
